title: The First Time Love Was Spoken… and Why It Will Break You Before It Heals You
paragraphs: The First Time Love Was Spoken… and Why It Will Break You Before It Heals You
You thought love began with tenderness. Scripture reveals it began with surrender.
There’s a moment in the Bible so quiet, so easily overlooked, that most people pass it without realizing they’ve just stepped into one of the deepest revelations of God’s heart.
Not in Genesis 1, where creation sings.
Not in the garden, where innocence breathes.
Not even in the first marriage, where Adam beholds Eve.
No… love waits.
It waits through chapters of beginnings, through the fall, through the flood, through generations of wandering hearts—until suddenly, in Genesis 22, it speaks.
And when it does… it doesn’t sound like what you expected.

“Take now your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love…”
Hebrew: קַח־נָא אֶת־בִּנְךָ אֶת־יְחִידְךָ אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ (kach-na et-bincha et-yechidcha asher ahavta)
The word for love here—אָהַב (ahav)—is not soft. It is not casual. It is not surface-level affection.
It is covenantal. Weighty. Costly.
The first time “love” appears in Scripture… it is tied to sacrifice.
Pause there.
Because this changes everything.

We live in a world that defines love by comfort, chemistry, and convenience. But the first time God lets us hear the word, He places it in the mouth of a Father… being asked to surrender the very thing He cherishes most.
Abraham had waited decades for Isaac. Every prayer, every promise, every tear of longing had led to this child.
And now God says… give him back.
This is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because if we’re honest, we don’t struggle with the idea of loving God—we struggle with what loving Him might cost us.

The text doesn’t soften the blow. It doesn’t explain away the tension. It simply shows a man rising early in the morning, carrying wood, walking in silence toward a mountain that feels more like a grave.

Isaac, unaware, asks a question that echoes through eternity:
“Where is the lamb?”

And Abraham responds with trembling faith:
“God will provide for Himself the lamb.”
Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה־לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה (Elohim yireh-lo ha-seh)
God will see. God will provide.
But Abraham doesn’t yet know how.
And neither do we, most of the time.
This is where love becomes real.
Not when it’s easy.
Not when it’s reciprocated.
But when you’re standing on the edge of losing something you prayed for… and still choosing to trust God anyway.
Be honest.
Have you ever loved God like that?
Or have you only loved Him when it didn’t hurt?
Because Genesis 22 is not just Abraham’s story.
It’s a mirror.
It exposes the quiet idols we don’t want to name.
The dreams we cling to tighter than obedience.
The blessings we fear losing more than we fear disobeying.
And yet… right at the breaking point—when the knife is raised, when heaven seems silent—God intervenes.
“Do not lay your hand on the boy…”
A ram is caught in the thicket.
A substitute is provided.
And suddenly, what looked like cruelty becomes revelation.
Because this was never about Isaac.
It was about showing us what love really is.
Fast forward centuries later… and another Father stands on another hill.
This time, there is no interruption.
No voice saying “stop.”
No ram in the thicket.
Because this time… the Son is the Lamb.

Greek, John 3:16:
Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον… (Houtōs gar ēgapēsen ho Theos ton kosmon)
“For God so loved the world…”
The word used here—ἀγαπάω (agapaō)—is the Greek fulfillment of ahav. A love that gives. A love that sacrifices. A love that doesn’t hold back.
The first mention of love in Genesis whispers.
The cross in the Gospels shouts.
God was never asking Abraham to do something He Himself wasn’t willing to do.
Let that settle in your spirit.
The same God who asked for Isaac… gave Jesus.
And this time, He didn’t spare Him.
Why?
Because He saw you.
Because He knew your sin, your shame, your hidden battles, your silent guilt—and still chose to love you anyway.
This is where the scandal turns into grace.
Because the truth is… we are not Isaac.
We are the ones who deserved the altar.
And yet Jesus stepped in as the substitute.
This is not just theology.
This is personal.
This is the moment where everything you’ve been hiding… meets everything God has already forgiven.
So what do you do with this kind of love?
You don’t just admire it.
You respond.
Maybe that response looks like surrendering something you’ve been holding too tightly.
Maybe it looks like repentance you’ve been avoiding.
Maybe it looks like finally admitting… you’ve been loving God on your terms, not His.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
Let this be the moment you remember.
The moment love stopped being a word… and became a cross.
If this stirred something in you, don’t keep it to yourself.
And if you feel your spirit leaning in… stay close.
There’s a deeper level too.
This isn’t about transactions.
It’s about transformation.
Supporting this mission helps keep truth moving, reaching hearts that are one message away from surrender.
If you want to be part of that… if you want your faith to be more than occasional inspiration… step in.
Because love was never meant to stay a concept.
It was meant to rewrite you.
And once you see it… you can’t go back to who you were before.
